chapters.title: Chapter 5: Putting Your Tax Plan Into Action

lessons.title: Declaring Investments to Your Employer and Submitting Proofs

children.text: You can make every right investment and still see a painfully small salary in February. That happens when your employer does not know about your investments, or does not believe you. For salaried taxpayers, tax is deducted from every paycheque based on what you tell HR, so the paperwork matters as much as the investments. This lesson walks through the full cycle: declaring, proving, and fixing anything missed when you file your return.

stats.label: Salary TDS certificate
stats.context: Replaced Form 16 under the Income-tax Rules, 2026

stats.label: Return due date
stats.context: For most salaried taxpayers, after the tax year ends

children.text: Under Section 392 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (192 under the 1961 Act), your employer must estimate your tax for the whole year and deduct it evenly from your salary. That estimate depends on two things you tell them: which regime you want, and which deductions you expect to claim.

body.latex: \text{Monthly TDS} = \frac{\text{Estimated Annual Tax} - \text{TDS Already Deducted}}{\text{Months Remaining in the Tax Year}}
body.caption: Employers recalculate this whenever your salary or declarations change, which is why a late correction can cause a sharp jump in the last few months.

body.title: A salaried taxpayer's year of tax paperwork

events.title: Choose your regime and declare
events.description: Tell HR whether you want the old or new regime. On the old regime, submit your planned deductions through Form 124 on the payroll portal.

events.title: TDS based on your declaration
events.description: Your employer deducts tax assuming your declared investments will happen. No proof is needed yet.

events.title: Proof submission window
events.description: Upload receipts, statements and certificates. Most employers set a hard cut-off date.

events.title: Final TDS adjustment
events.description: Claims without valid proof are removed, and any shortfall in tax is deducted from your last few salaries.

events.title: Form 130 issued
events.description: Your employer gives you Form 130 showing salary, deductions allowed and tax deducted for the year.

events.title: File your return
events.description: Claim anything your employer missed, and confirm your final choice of regime.

children.text: Step 1: Tell Your Employer Your Regime

body.title: What your regime declaration changes on your payslip

columns.label: You declare the old regime
points: Employer asks for Form 124 with planned deductions
Section 123 (80C), 124(3) NPS, 126 (80D), HRA and home loan interest are factored into TDS
Lower monthly TDS if your deductions are large
Proofs are required later in the year

columns.label: You declare the new regime, or say nothing
points: New regime under Section 202 applies by default
Most deductions are ignored for TDS
Employer NPS up to 14% of salary is still considered

body.text: Your declaration to HR only decides how TDS is calculated during the year. It does not lock you in. If you have no business income, you can pick either regime when you file your return, as long as you file by the due date. File late, and the new regime applies with no option to switch.

children.text: Form 124 has two parts: Part A for your basic details and Part B for the benefits you are claiming. In practice, most employers put it on a payroll portal like Keka, greytHR or Darwinbox, so you fill fields rather than a PDF. Compared with the old Form 12BB, it adds one notable requirement: you must disclose your relationship with your landlord if you claim HRA.

body.caption: What Form 124 asks for, and what proof you will need later

cells: Amount for each investment or payment
PPF passbook, ELSS statement, LIC receipts, tuition fee receipts, NSC certificate, home loan principal certificate
Premiums for family and parents, ages
Health insurance premium receipts, check-up bills
Landlord name, address, rent, relationship; landlord PAN if yearly rent exceeds ₹1 lakh
Lender name, address, PAN, interest amount
Tickets, boarding passes or travel invoices

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: Under the Income-tax Rules, 2026, the salary TDS certificate you once knew as Form 16 is now Form ___.
body.explanation: Form 16 became Form 130, the investment declaration Form 12BB became Form 124, and Form 26AS became Form 168 from tax year 2026-27.

children.text: Step 3: Submit Proofs Before the Cut-Off

cards.definition: Passbook page or bank statement showing the deposit date and amount in the tax year.
Account statement from the AMC, CAMS or KFintech showing purchase dates and amounts. A screenshot of an app home screen is usually rejected.
Premium paid receipt for the tax year, showing the policy number and the insured person's name.
Receipt or fee certificate from the school or college showing the tuition component separately.
Provisional or final certificate from the lender showing principal and interest separately.
No proof needed. Your employer already deducts it and includes it automatically.

children.text: Declared more than you could prove? The shortfall does not vanish; it lands on your last few salaries.

body.caption: Kiran, a sales manager in Bhubaneswar, old regime, 30% slab: declared ₹1,50,000 of 80C in April, proved only ₹90,000 in February

body.title: Your Turn: The February Shock
body.prompt: If Kiran's employer recovers the extra ₹18,720 evenly across January, February and March, how much additional TDS is deducted from each of those salaries?
body.explanation: ₹18,720 ÷ 3 = ₹6,240 extra each month, on top of his normal TDS. Had he declared a realistic figure in April, the extra tax would have been spread over 12 months at ₹1,560 a month instead.

body.label: Why accurate declarations matter
body.context: The same ₹18,720 costs ₹1,560 a month when spread over 12 months, but ₹6,240 a month when squeezed into the last 3.

body.title: Missed the Deadline
body.question: Priya, an HR executive in Indore on the old regime, invests ₹1,00,000 in ELSS on 20 March, after her company's proof cut-off. Her Form 130 does not include it, so extra TDS was deducted. What can she do?
options: Nothing; the deduction is lost for this year
Claim the ₹1,00,000 under Section 123 (80C) in her return filed by 31 July, and get the excess TDS refunded
Ask her employer to reissue Form 130 in August
Carry the deduction forward to next year
body.explanation: The employer's calculation is provisional. Priya can claim any valid deduction directly in her return. The extra TDS will come back as a refund once the return is processed. She should keep the ELSS statement as proof in case the department asks.

body.text: Your employer's TDS is only an estimate. Your income tax return is where your final tax is decided.

children.text: Step 4: Check Everything Before You File

Before filing, compare three documents: Form 130 from your employer, your Annual Tax Statement (Form 168, which replaces Form 26AS from tax year 2026-27) and your Annual Information Statement (AIS) on the income tax portal. The TDS in Form 130 should match what appears in Form 168. Interest income and mutual fund transactions in the AIS should match what you report.

body.title: Scenario: The New Joiner
body.scenario: Aditi joined a fintech startup in Bengaluru in October after leaving her previous employer in September. At her old job she had declared the old regime and submitted ₹1,50,000 of 80C proofs. At the new job, HR onboarding was rushed and she never declared a regime, so the new regime was applied by default. Both employers deducted TDS without knowing about each other's salary. She now has two Form 130s.
body.prompt: What problems might Aditi face, and how should she handle them?
body.modelAnswer: Two problems. First, each employer calculated TDS as if its salary was her only income, so each may have applied lower slabs and the full benefit of the standard deduction and rebate separately. Her combined income is likely to face more tax than was deducted, so she may owe tax when filing. Second, the two employers used different regimes. Neither declaration is binding: when she files her return by 31 July, she chooses one regime for the whole year, based on her total salary and total deductions. She should add up income and TDS from both Form 130s, check them against Form 168 and her AIS, compare her tax under both regimes, pay any balance as self-assessment tax before filing, and claim her ₹1,50,000 under Section 123 (80C) only if the old regime works out cheaper. For the future, she should give a new employer details of her previous salary and TDS so that TDS for the rest of the year is calculated correctly.

body.title: Your Year-Round Tax Paperwork Routine
steps: April: compare your tax under both regimes and declare your choice to HR
April: fill Form 124 on your payroll portal with realistic, not hopeful, figures
Throughout the year: save every receipt and statement in one folder as you invest
December: check whether your actual investments match your declaration, and update it if not
Before the cut-off: upload clear, complete proofs for every claim
June: download Form 130 and check it against Form 168 and your AIS
By 31 July: file your return, claim anything missed and confirm your regime

points: Under Section 392 (192), your employer deducts TDS monthly based on your declared regime and deductions.
Form 124 replaced Form 12BB for declarations; Form 130 replaced Form 16; Form 168 replaced Form 26AS from tax year 2026-27.
Declare realistic figures in April, because unproved claims are clawed back from your last few salaries.
Your regime declaration to HR is not final; salaried taxpayers can choose either regime in a return filed by the due date.
Deductions missed by your employer can still be claimed in your return, with excess TDS refunded.
If you change jobs mid-year, share previous salary details with your new employer and reconcile both Form 130s when filing.

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and is not tax or legal advice. Form numbers, due dates and procedures reflect the Income-tax Act, 2025 and Income-tax Rules, 2026 as understood at the time of writing, and employer processes vary. Consult a qualified Chartered Accountant for decisions specific to your situation.
